investigator.method: Level 1 PASSIVE_STATIC only: plain curl GETs (descriptive User-Agent, no authentication, no browser) of the venue's own homepage. wp-content/wp-json signals confirmed WordPress; the standard, publicly-exposed wp/v2 REST API root (/wp-json/) was fetched to enumerate real registered namespaces/post types (no guessed private endpoint), which listed a custom post type literally named 'events' — this project's documented WordPress 'The Events Calendar' Tribe endpoint (/wp-json/tribe/events/v1/events) was tried first per this task's own instructions and returned 404 (not that plugin), so the site's own actual custom 'events' type (/wp-json/wp/v2/events) was used instead, all via plain unauthenticated GETs.

probe_history.reason: A plain curl GET of https://heimathafen-neukoelln.de/wp-json/wp/v2/events?per_page=5 (a standard, publicly-documented WordPress REST API endpoint for a custom post type the site's own /wp-json/ root and /wp-json/wp/v2/types both confirm exist) returned 200 with 5 real event records, each with title/content/link/id plus a rich ACF field set (event_performances[].performance_date_time/performance_ticket, event_prices[]). This directly answers the investigation question at Level 1 — no structural/browser escalation was needed. (The Tribe 'The Events Calendar' endpoint this project usually tries first, /wp-json/tribe/events/v1/events, was also tried and correctly returned 404 — this site uses its own custom 'events' post type instead, not that plugin.)

venue_reference: Heimathafen Neukölln (theatre / concert / cultural venue, Neukölln, Berlin — Karl-Marx-Straße 141, 12043 Berlin)

identity.notes: The venue's own homepage <title> ('Heimathafen Neukölln – Theater in Berlin Neukölln'), meta description, and retained body text ('Karl-Marx-Straße 141, 12043 Berlin') all self-identify directly and match the venue's well-known real-world address in Neukölln, Berlin.

site_classification.platform: WordPress (wp-content/wp-json signals confirmed), with a custom 'events' post type (not the Tribe 'The Events Calendar' plugin — that endpoint 404s) exposed via the standard wp/v2 REST API and enriched with Advanced Custom Fields (ACF) data (the site's own /wp-json/ root lists an active 'acf/v3' namespace).

title.notes: Each event record's own 'title.rendered' field, stated directly (HTML entities like '&' decode mechanically to '&').

start_date.notes: Each event's own 'acf.event_performances[].performance_date_time' field is a free-text string (e.g. 'LENA & LINUS': '03/05/2027 8:00 p.m.') with slash-separated numbers whose month/day order is not self-evident from that one string alone. However, the SAME retained field, across the SAME sampled response, contains multiple other values whose first number exceeds 12 and therefore cannot be a month index: 'STREIT & ZUVERSICHT': '09/29/2026' (29 cannot be a month), 'EB DAVIS & THE SUPERBAND...': '11/27/2026' (27 cannot be a month), 'BAC': '02/19/2027' (19 cannot be a month). These three retained values mechanically prove this field's own consistent numeric convention is <month>/<day>/<year> across this sample — not a plausibility judgement, a structural constraint of the numbers themselves. Applying that proven convention to 'LENA & LINUS'’s own '03/05/2027' yields exactly one result: month 03 (March), day 05, year 2027.

derivation.rule: Within the retained wp/v2/events API sample, every 'acf.event_performances[].performance_date_time' value shares one slash-separated <A>/<B>/<year> format. At least three sampled values have A > 12 (09/29/2026, 11/27/2026, 02/19/2027), which is structurally impossible for a month component, mechanically proving A is the month and B is the day for every value sharing this same field/format in this sample, including values where both A and B are individually <= 12. Parse the target value's A as month and B as day, both zero-padded, concatenated with the year as <year>-<A>-<B>.
inputs: 09/29/2026 (STREIT & ZUVERSICHT, disambiguating: 29 cannot be a month)
11/27/2026 (EB DAVIS & THE SUPERBAND, disambiguating: 27 cannot be a month)

time.notes: The time-of-day portion of the same 'performance_date_time' string ('8:00 p.m.') is stated directly and unambiguously (12-hour clock with an explicit am/pm marker, no month/day-style ambiguity). No UTC offset or IANA timezone is stated anywhere, so this is honestly a floating local time (presumed Europe/Berlin), never upgraded to a UTC instant. A separate free-text 'performance_description' field on the same record ('Einlass ab 19:00 Uhr (Saal)') gives a door/admission time, not the performance start time, and was not conflated with it.

end.notes: No end time or end date field is exposed anywhere in the sampled ACF event data.

venue_location.notes: This is a single-venue site with no per-record venue/location ACF field on the events API response. The venue's own homepage states its full name and address directly in one retained block ('Karl-Marx-Straße 141, 12043 Berlin').

source_record_id.notes: Each event's own WordPress post 'id' field, directly stated. WordPress post IDs are permanent, auto-incrementing, platform-native identifiers by WordPress's own well-documented design (they are never reassigned or regenerated for an existing post) — the same class of platform-native stable-identifier reasoning already accepted for razzmatazz-barcelona-01's Sanity '_id' and kesselhaus-kulturbrauerei-berlin-01's Firebase push id.

event_url.notes: Each event's own 'link' field, stated directly.

price.notes: Each event's own 'acf.event_prices[].event_prices_price' field, stated directly as a German-formatted price string (comma decimal separator, Euro sign) — retained as-is, not parsed into a numeric+currency pair by this investigation. A companion 'event_prices_label' field ('Tickets') is also present. At least one sampled record's own 'acf.event_text_fields' explicitly states 'Kein Kartenverkauf über den Heimathafen Neukölln' (no ticket sales through the venue itself for that record) — a genuine per-record exception, not fabricated.

blockers.description: The date-format disambiguation for 'performance_date_time' (proving MM/DD/YYYY from within-sample examples with day > 12) was demonstrated on this one 5-record sample. A production parser should keep re-validating that assumption defensively (e.g. reject/flag any record where BOTH numbers are <= 12 AND the ambiguity cannot be independently cross-checked) rather than hard-coding it as permanently guaranteed.
